key_terms.meaning: Movement of a component caused by a concentration difference.
A phase or material that blocks one component more than another, so a separation is possible.
Adding a solvent, gas or other phase that selectively takes up a component.
Making a new phase by heating, cooling or vaporizing so components divide between phases.
An adsorbent, ion-exchange resin or similar solid that selectively holds a component.
Velocity of species i measured relative to the molar-average velocity of the mixture.
Moles of species i crossing unit area per unit time, N<sub>i</sub> = c<sub>i</sub> u<sub>i</sub>.
J<sub>A</sub> = -D<sub>AB</sub> dC<sub>A</sub>/dz for binary diffusion; J<sub>A</sub> is diffusion flux relative to the mixture.
∂C<sub>A</sub>/∂t = D<sub>AB</sub> ∂²C<sub>A</sub>/∂z² for constant D, no reaction and one-dimensional diffusion.
N<sub>A</sub> = −N<sub>B</sub>, so N<sub>A</sub> = D<sub>AB</sub> c (y<sub>A1</sub> − y<sub>A2</sub>)/L and the profile is a straight line.
(y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub> = (y<sub>B2</sub> - y<sub>B1</sub>)/ln(y<sub>B2</sub>/y<sub>B1</sub>), the factor that corrects stagnant-B diffusion.
t = ρ<sub>L</sub> (y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub> (z² − z₀²)/[2 M D c (y<sub>A1</sub> − y<sub>A2</sub>)] for a falling liquid level; read backwards it gives D.
Treat a slowly moving boundary as steady at each instant and integrate over time.
D<sub>AB</sub> = 7.4×10⁻⁸ (φ M<sub>B</sub>)<sup>1/2</sup> T/(μ<sub>B</sub> V<sub>A</sub><sup>0.6</sup>) cm²/s, for a dilute solute in a liquid.
D<sub>AB</sub>, in m²/s, the property that measures how easily A diffuses through B.
D = D₀ exp(-E<sub>a</sub>/(RT)) for solid diffusion, where E<sub>a</sub> is activation energy.
Pore diffusion controlled by molecule–wall collisions: D<sub>K</sub> = 97 r (T/M)<sup>1/2</sup> m²/s, independent of pressure.
Multicomponent flux relations in which every pair i-j has its own diffusivity D<sub>ij</sub>.
D<sub>i,mixture</sub> = (1 - y<sub>i</sub>)/Σ(y<sub>j</sub>/D<sub>ij</sub>), useful for a dilute species i in a multicomponent gas.
Fo<sub>m</sub> = D t/L², the dimensionless time used in unsteady diffusion.

takeaways: Most separations, apart from mechanical ones, work by giving one component a second phase to move into; how that phase is obtained sorts them into phase creation, phase addition, barrier and solid agent.
Fick's first law links diffusion flux to the negative concentration gradient; Fick's second law adds conservation of mass to give concentration versus time.
Equimolar counter-diffusion uses the plain mole-fraction difference, while stagnant-B diffusion is larger by the factor 1/(y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub>.
When the diffusion area changes, the total rate stays constant but the flux changes, so Fick's law must be integrated over the geometry.
Pseudo-steady treatment works when a boundary moves slowly enough that each instant can be solved as a steady problem.
D is measured in a known geometry or predicted from kinetic theory and group correlations; solid D values are small and rise steeply with temperature.
With three or more species, each flux depends on all gradients, and Stefan–Maxwell or Wilke relations are needed.
Unsteady diffusion answers come as charts, series or error functions, organized by dimensionless groups such as Fo<sub>m</sub>.
bank_note: Long answers usually ask for the classification of operations, the two Fick laws with their assumptions, the stagnant and equimolar derivations, variable-area and pseudo-steady integration (the Stefan tube), diffusivity measurement and prediction, and solid, multicomponent and unsteady diffusion.

bank.q: Classify mass transfer operations by the way the second phase is obtained (phase creation, phase addition, barrier, solid agent) and by the phases in contact. Give an industrial example of each and name the usual contactor.
outline: Define mass transfer and say why a second phase is needed
Four families with the mechanism of each
Place one stated operation on the scheme
answer: Mass transfer is the movement of one component through a mixture, or from one phase into another, because its concentration (strictly its chemical potential) differs from place to place. A single phase cannot be split this way: separation needs a second phase that takes up the wanted component more, or less, than the feed does. Mechanical separations such as filtration and centrifuging are a different subject.

answer.text: The four families differ only in how the second phase is obtained:

head: Family
How the second phase appears
Operations
Industrial example
rows: heat or work makes it out of the feed
a foreign liquid or gas (a separating agent) is brought in
CO₂ scrubbing with an amine; oil from seeds with hexane
a membrane passes one species faster
a solid takes up the solute on its surface or sites
solvent vapour on activated carbon; water softening on a resin

answer: Drying with hot gas is usually put under phase creation, because the heat turns the water into vapour; it is not a solid-agent operation, since the solid gives up water instead of taking up a solute.

answer.text: A second sorting uses the phases that touch, because each pair brings its own equilibrium data and equipment:

head: Phases in contact
Operations
rows: leaching, ion exchange, crystallization, adsorption from solution

answer: A third sorting is by contactor. A stage-wise contactor (a tray column, a mixer-settler) mixes the phases, lets them approach equilibrium and separates them, so composition changes in steps. A differential contactor (a packed tower, a wetted wall, a spray) keeps the phases in continuous contact, so composition changes smoothly along the path. Either can run batch or continuous.

Placing an operation: for CO₂ removal from flue gas the CO₂ moves from the gas into an amine solution that is brought in from outside, so it is absorption, under phase addition, a gas–liquid pair, usually in a packed tower. With 22 mol% CO₂ at 1 atm and 300 K the gas holds c = 101325/(8.314 × 300) = 40.6 mol/m³ in all and 0.22 × 40.6 = 8.93 mol/m³ of CO₂, the load the solvent must take up.

Check: every operation in the table names the component that moves, the phase it leaves, the phase it enters and how that second phase was made; an answer that names only the equipment ("a packed tower") has not classified anything.

bank.q: Define species velocity, molar average velocity, diffusion velocity, molar flux and diffusion flux for a binary mixture. Show that N<sub>A</sub> = J<sub>A</sub> + y<sub>A</sub>(N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub>) and that J<sub>A</sub> = −J<sub>B</sub>. Distinguish molecular and eddy diffusion.
outline: v<sub>i</sub>, u, v<sub>i</sub> − u with units
N<sub>i</sub> = c<sub>i</sub> v<sub>i</sub>, J<sub>i</sub> = c<sub>i</sub>(v<sub>i</sub> − u), n<sub>i</sub> = M<sub>i</sub> N<sub>i</sub>
Derivation of the split into diffusion and bulk flow
Molecular versus eddy diffusion; D<sub>E</sub> is not a property
answer: Species velocity v<sub>i</sub> (m/s) is the average velocity of molecules of i past a plane fixed in the laboratory. With molar concentration c<sub>i</sub> (mol/m³), the molar flux of i in the fixed frame is N<sub>i</sub> = c<sub>i</sub> v<sub>i</sub>, in mol/(m²·s); the mass flux is n<sub>i</sub> = ρ<sub>i</sub> v<sub>i</sub> = M<sub>i</sub> N<sub>i</sub>, in kg/(m²·s).

The molar average velocity is the concentration-weighted mean u = (c<sub>A</sub> v<sub>A</sub> + c<sub>B</sub> v<sub>B</sub>)/c = (N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub>)/c, with c = c<sub>A</sub> + c<sub>B</sub>. The diffusion velocity of A is v<sub>A</sub> − u, its velocity relative to the moving mixture, and the diffusion flux is J<sub>A</sub> = c<sub>A</sub>(v<sub>A</sub> − u), also in mol/(m²·s).

answer.text: Split the fixed-frame flux by adding and subtracting c<sub>A</sub> u:
answer.pre:
N<sub>A</sub> = c<sub>A</sub> v<sub>A</sub> = c<sub>A</sub> u + c<sub>A</sub>(v<sub>A</sub> − u)
    = (c<sub>A</sub>/c)(N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub>) + J<sub>A</sub>
    = J<sub>A</sub> + y<sub>A</sub>(N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub>)

answer: The first term is diffusion relative to the mixture; the second, y<sub>A</sub>(N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub>), is A carried along by the bulk motion of the mixture. They are equal in size only by accident; at high y<sub>A</sub> the bulk term can dominate.

answer.pre: J<sub>A</sub> + J<sub>B</sub> = c<sub>A</sub> v<sub>A</sub> + c<sub>B</sub> v<sub>B</sub> − (c<sub>A</sub> + c<sub>B</sub>) u = (N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub>) − c u = 0

answer: So J<sub>A</sub> = −J<sub>B</sub> always, while N<sub>A</sub> = −N<sub>B</sub> only when N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub> = 0 (equimolar counter-diffusion).

answer.text: Numerical check with c = 40.6 mol/m³, y<sub>A</sub> = 0.30, N<sub>A</sub> = 3.0×10⁻³ and N<sub>B</sub> = 1.0×10⁻³ mol/(m²·s):

answer: Molecular diffusion is the random thermal motion of molecules; it acts even in a fluid at rest and is described by D<sub>AB</sub>, a property of the pair at given T and P. Eddy diffusion is the mixing caused by turbulent eddies carrying lumps of fluid; it is modelled as J<sub>A</sub>(eddy) = −D<sub>E</sub> dc<sub>A</sub>/dz, where the eddy diffusivity D<sub>E</sub> depends on the flow, the geometry and the distance from the wall, and falls to zero at a solid wall where the eddies die out. In turbulent flow D<sub>E</sub> can be thousands of times D<sub>AB</sub> in the core, so the molecular step near the wall controls the rate.
Check: J<sub>A</sub> + J<sub>B</sub> = 1.8×10⁻³ − 1.8×10⁻³ = 0, and J<sub>A</sub>/c<sub>A</sub> = 1.8×10⁻³/12.18 = 1.48×10⁻⁴ m/s equals the diffusion velocity found directly.

bank.q: State Fick's first law in its general molar form and in the constant-concentration form. Derive Fick's second law from a balance on a thin slab, extend it to a reacting system and state the initial and boundary conditions a solution needs.
outline: J<sub>A</sub> = −c D<sub>AB</sub> dy<sub>A</sub>/dz and J<sub>A</sub> = −D<sub>AB</sub> dc<sub>A</sub>/dz
Slab balance and the limit Δz → 0
Form with variable D and reaction R<sub>A</sub>
One initial and two boundary conditions, with examples
Steady state gives a straight line
answer: Fick's first law: J<sub>A</sub> = −c D<sub>AB</sub> dy<sub>A</sub>/dz, where J<sub>A</sub> is the molar diffusion flux relative to the molar average velocity (mol/(m²·s)), c the total molar concentration (mol/m³), D<sub>AB</sub> the binary diffusivity (m²/s) and y<sub>A</sub> the mole fraction. When c is constant (a gas at fixed T and P), c dy<sub>A</sub>/dz = dc<sub>A</sub>/dz and J<sub>A</sub> = −D<sub>AB</sub> dc<sub>A</sub>/dz. The minus sign says A moves down its gradient.

Slab balance: take a slab of area S and thickness Δz with no flow and no reaction. In a time Δt, moles in at z minus moles out at z + Δz equal the gain inside: [J<sub>A</sub>(z) − J<sub>A</sub>(z + Δz)] S Δt = S Δz Δc<sub>A</sub>.

answer.text: Divide by S Δz Δt and let Δz, Δt → 0:

answer: With a homogeneous reaction producing A at R<sub>A</sub> mol/(m³·s) (negative when A is consumed), the balance gains a source term: ∂c<sub>A</sub>/∂t = ∂/∂z(D<sub>AB</sub> ∂c<sub>A</sub>/∂z) + R<sub>A</sub>. For a first-order consumption R<sub>A</sub> = −k c<sub>A</sub> at steady state, D d²c<sub>A</sub>/dz² = k c<sub>A</sub>, whose solution is a sum of exponentials, not a straight line.

The equation is first order in t and second order in z, so it needs one initial condition, for example c<sub>A</sub>(z, 0) = c₀, and two boundary conditions, one at each face. Common ones: a fixed surface value c<sub>A</sub>(0, t) = c<sub>s</sub>; a sealed face ∂c<sub>A</sub>/∂z = 0; a fixed flux; or a convective face −D ∂c<sub>A</sub>/∂z = k<sub>c</sub>(c<sub>s</sub> − c<sub>bulk</sub>).
Steady state, constant D, no reaction: d²c<sub>A</sub>/dz² = 0, so c<sub>A</sub> = a + bz, a straight line fixed by the two face values.

Numerical check: for y<sub>A</sub> = 0.30 at z = 0 and 0.10 at z = 4 mm in a gas with c = 40.6 mol/m³ and D<sub>AB</sub> = 1.8×10⁻⁵ m²/s, dc<sub>A</sub>/dz = 40.6 × (−0.20/0.004) = −2030 mol/m⁴ and J<sub>A</sub> = 1.8×10⁻⁵ × 2030 = 3.65×10⁻² mol/(m²·s). On the straight line every slice carries the same J<sub>A</sub>, so ∂J<sub>A</sub>/∂z = 0 and nothing accumulates: the steady second law is satisfied.

bank.q: Derive the steady flux for (a) equimolar counter-diffusion and (b) diffusion of A through stagnant B in a binary gas film. Explain the log-mean factor and compare the two for y<sub>A</sub> = 0.20 and 0.05 at the faces of a 5 mm film (c = 40.6 mol/m³, D<sub>AB</sub> = 1.8×10⁻⁵ m²/s).
outline: General flux with the bulk term
Equimolar: bulk term zero, straight profile
Stagnant B: separate and integrate, ln form and log-mean form
Numbers for both cases and the profiles
answer: Start from N<sub>A</sub> = −c D<sub>AB</sub> dy<sub>A</sub>/dz + y<sub>A</sub>(N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub>), steady and one-dimensional, so N<sub>A</sub> and N<sub>B</sub> are constant across the film; c and D<sub>AB</sub> are constant.

(a) Equimolar counter-diffusion: N<sub>A</sub> = −N<sub>B</sub>, the bulk term vanishes, N<sub>A</sub> = −c D<sub>AB</sub> dy<sub>A</sub>/dz. Integrating from z = 0 (y<sub>A1</sub>) to z = L (y<sub>A2</sub>): N<sub>A</sub> = c D<sub>AB</sub> (y<sub>A1</sub> − y<sub>A2</sub>)/L. The profile is a straight line.

answer.text: (b) Stagnant B: N<sub>B</sub> = 0, so N<sub>A</sub>(1 − y<sub>A</sub>) = −c D<sub>AB</sub> dy<sub>A</sub>/dz. Separate and integrate:
answer.pre:
N<sub>A</sub> ∫₀ᴸ dz = −c D<sub>AB</sub> ∫ dy<sub>A</sub>/(1 − y<sub>A</sub>)
N<sub>A</sub> = (c D<sub>AB</sub>/L) ln[(1 − y<sub>A2</sub>)/(1 − y<sub>A1</sub>)] = (c D<sub>AB</sub>/L) ln(y<sub>B2</sub>/y<sub>B1</sub>)
    = c D<sub>AB</sub> (y<sub>A1</sub> − y<sub>A2</sub>)/[L (y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub>],   (y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub> = (y<sub>B2</sub> − y<sub>B1</sub>)/ln(y<sub>B2</sub>/y<sub>B1</sub>)

answer: The log mean appears because y<sub>B1</sub> − y<sub>B2</sub> = y<sub>A2</sub> − y<sub>A1</sub>, so the ln form can be multiplied and divided by the difference. Since every y<sub>B</sub> < 1, (y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub> < 1 and 1/(y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub> > 1: as A diffuses it drags the mixture with it, and B must diffuse back against that drift at the same rate to stay still. The drift carries extra A.

The stagnant-B flux is 1/0.873 = 1.146 times the equimolar value: about 15 % more, because y<sub>A</sub> is not small. The stagnant profile is exponential in y<sub>B</sub> and bows slightly above the straight line.

For a liquid film use x for y and the solution molar density for c (about 5.5×10⁴ mol/m³ for dilute aqueous solutions), averaged over the two faces. For 9 % and 3 % acetic acid across 1 mm of water at 17 °C (D = 0.95×10⁻⁹ m²/s) this gives (x<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub> = 0.981 and N<sub>A</sub> = 1.02×10⁻³ mol/(m²·s).
Check: (c D/L) × 0.1719 = 0.1462 × 0.1719 = 0.0251 by the ln form, the same as 0.0219/0.873 by the log-mean form.

bank.q: Ammonia diffuses through a 2.0 mm stagnant film of air towards water that absorbs it, at 298 K and 1 atm. Its partial pressure is 10.0 kPa at the outer edge of the film and 2.0 kPa at the water surface. D = 2.3×10⁻⁵ m²/s. Find the flux of ammonia in mol/(m²·s) and kg/(m²·h), compare it with equimolar counter-diffusion and find y<sub>A</sub> at mid-film.
outline: c = P/RT and the mole fractions
N<sub>A</sub> by the log-mean and ln forms
answer: Air does not dissolve, so it is stagnant: N<sub>B</sub> = 0 and the stagnant-B formula applies.

answer.text: Model: steady, one-dimensional, ideal gas, constant D and c across the film. Start from N<sub>A</sub> = −c D dy<sub>A</sub>/dz + y<sub>A</sub>(N<sub>A</sub> + N<sub>B</sub>) with N<sub>B</sub> = 0, separate the variables and integrate across the film thickness L:
answer.pre:
N<sub>A</sub> (1 − y<sub>A</sub>) = −c D dy<sub>A</sub>/dz
N<sub>A</sub> = (c D/L) ln[(1 − y<sub>A2</sub>)/(1 − y<sub>A1</sub>)] = c D (y<sub>A1</sub> − y<sub>A2</sub>)/[L (y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub>]

answer: Equimolar value for comparison: c D (y<sub>A1</sub> − y<sub>A2</sub>)/L = 40.9 × 2.3×10⁻⁵ × 0.0790/0.002 = 3.71×10⁻² mol/(m²·s).
Mass flux: 3.95×10⁻² mol/(m²·s) × 0.017 kg/mol × 3600 s/h = 2.42 kg/(m²·h).

Mid-film: y<sub>B</sub> = y<sub>B1</sub>(y<sub>B2</sub>/y<sub>B1</sub>)<sup>0.5</sup> = 0.9013 × (1.0877)<sup>0.5</sup> = 0.9400, so y<sub>A</sub> = 0.0600, slightly above the straight-line value 0.0592.

Meaning: the water surface acts as a sink, so y<sub>A2</sub> is set by the small ammonia pressure over the solution; if the water were saturated, y<sub>A2</sub> would rise towards y<sub>A1</sub> and the flux would fall to zero. Doubling the film thickness (slower gas, poorer mixing) halves the flux, which is why absorbers make the gas film thin.
Units check: c D/L has units (mol/m³)(m²/s)/m = mol/(m²·s), and the log term is dimensionless, so the flux needs no further conversion; only the mass flux needs M in kg/mol.
Check: the stagnant flux is 6.4 % above the equimolar one, matching 1/0.940 = 1.064; the correction is small because the ammonia is fairly dilute (below 10 mol%).

bank.q: A gas A diffuses equimolarly through a conical duct 0.20 m long whose radius grows linearly from 10 mm to 25 mm. At 300 K the partial pressure of A is 20 kPa at the narrow end and 5 kPa at the wide end; D<sub>AB</sub> = 1.6×10⁻⁵ m²/s. Derive the rate and find it, and the fluxes at the two ends.
outline: W = A(z) N<sub>A</sub> constant at steady state
A(z) = π r(z)², r linear in z
W = π r₁ r₂ D (c<sub>A1</sub> − c<sub>A2</sub>)/L
answer: At steady state nothing accumulates, so the molar rate W (mol/s) is the same through every cross-section, while the flux N<sub>A</sub> = W/A(z) changes with the area. For equimolar counter-diffusion W = −D<sub>AB</sub> A(z) dc<sub>A</sub>/dz.

Assumptions: the two vessels at the ends are large and well mixed, so the end concentrations stay fixed; the gas is ideal at constant T and P, so c and D<sub>AB</sub> are constant; A and B cross in equal and opposite amounts, so there is no bulk term; and the taper is gentle, so the concentration is uniform over each cross-section and the problem stays one-dimensional.
Geometry: r(z) = r₁ + (r₂ − r₁) z/L, so A(z) = π r(z)². Separate: W dz/A(z) = −D<sub>AB</sub> dc<sub>A</sub>.

answer.pre:
∫₀ᴸ dz/(π r²) = [L/(π (r₂ − r₁))] (1/r₁ − 1/r₂) = L/(π r₁ r₂)
W = π r₁ r₂ D<sub>AB</sub> (c<sub>A1</sub> − c<sub>A2</sub>)/L

answer: Concentrations: c<sub>A1</sub> = 20000/(8.314 × 300) = 8.02 mol/m³ and c<sub>A2</sub> = 5000/(8.314 × 300) = 2.00 mol/m³, so Δc<sub>A</sub> = 6.01 mol/m³.

End fluxes: narrow end N<sub>A</sub> = 3.78×10⁻⁷/(π × 0.010²) = 1.20×10⁻³ mol/(m²·s); wide end N<sub>A</sub> = 3.78×10⁻⁷/(π × 0.025²) = 1.92×10⁻⁴ mol/(m²·s). The ratio is (25/10)² = 6.25, as the areas require.

Comparison: a straight tube of radius 10 mm would carry 1.51×10⁻⁷ mol/s and one of 25 mm 9.45×10⁻⁷ mol/s. The cone behaves like a straight tube of radius √(r₁ r₂) = 15.8 mm, and the narrow end, where the flux is highest, controls the rate.

If B were stagnant instead, the same separation would give W ∫dz/A = (c D<sub>AB</sub>) ln[(1 − y<sub>A2</sub>)/(1 − y<sub>A1</sub>)], so the geometry factor L/(π r₁ r₂) is unchanged and only the driving term changes: the geometry and the driving force always separate, which is the point of the method.
Check: π r₁ r₂ = π × (15.8 mm)² confirms the equivalent radius, and W lies between the two straight-tube values.

bank.q: Benzene evaporates from a narrow vertical tube into air that sweeps the open top, at 298 K and 1 atm. Its vapour pressure is 12.7 kPa, liquid density 880 kg/m³, M = 78 g/mol, D = 9.6×10⁻⁶ m²/s. Using pseudo-steady state, derive the time for the level to fall from 20 mm to 50 mm below the top, and evaluate it.
outline: Flux at a given path z
answer: Air does not dissolve in benzene, so air is stagnant in the tube. At the liquid surface y<sub>A1</sub> = 12.7/101.325 = 0.1253; at the top the sweeping air keeps y<sub>A2</sub> = 0. c = 101325/(8.314 × 298) = 40.9 mol/m³.
When the gas path is z, the stagnant-B flux is N<sub>A</sub> = D c (y<sub>A1</sub> − y<sub>A2</sub>)/[z (y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub>].
The level falls because this flux removes liquid: (ρ<sub>L</sub>/M) dz/dt = N<sub>A</sub>, so (ρ<sub>L</sub>/M) z dz = [D c (y<sub>A1</sub> − y<sub>A2</sub>)/(y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub>] dt.

At the start (z = 20 mm) the flux is 9.6×10⁻⁶ × 40.9 × 0.1253/(0.020 × 0.936) = 2.63×10⁻³ mol/(m²·s), and the level falls at N<sub>A</sub> M/ρ<sub>L</sub> = 2.63×10⁻³ × 0.078/880 = 2.3×10⁻⁷ m/s, or 0.84 mm/h. The rate falls as the path grows, since N<sub>A</sub> ∝ 1/z.

Pseudo-steady check: the vapour held in the gas column (about y<sub>A</sub> c/2 = 2.6 mol/m³ on average) is tiny against the liquid that evaporates (ρ<sub>L</sub>/M = 1.13×10⁴ mol/m³), a ratio near 2×10⁻⁴, so the profile keeps up with the moving surface.

Exam variant: if the question gives the level fall and the time and asks for D, the same equation is solved for D. With 30 mm of fall in 62.6 h it returns D = 9.6×10⁻⁶ m²/s, which is how Winkelmann's method measures diffusivity.

Assumptions behind the result: the tube is isothermal; the process is quasi-steady, because the level falls slowly compared with the time the gas profile needs to settle; air does not dissolve in benzene; and the sweeping air keeps the benzene partial pressure at the mouth near zero. This apparatus, the Stefan tube, is also the standard way to measure D<sub>AB</sub>: a plot of t against z² − z₀² is a straight line whose slope gives D.
Check: halving D would double the time; the time depends on z² − z₀² = 2.1×10⁻³ m², not on the 30 mm fall alone.

bank.q: A vapour A at y<sub>A</sub> = 0.05 diffuses through a stagnant gas mixture of B (y = 0.40), C (0.35) and D (0.20) at 300 K and 1 atm. D<sub>AB</sub> = 6.0×10⁻⁵, D<sub>AC</sub> = 1.9×10⁻⁵ and D<sub>AD</sub> = 2.2×10⁻⁵ m²/s. Find the effective diffusivity of A by Wilke's equation, and the flux across a 1.5 mm film over which y<sub>A</sub> falls from 0.05 to 0.01.
outline: Wilke's equation and when it holds
D<sub>A,m</sub>; the A-free basis gives the same
Stagnant-mixture flux with the bulk term
Compare with a wrong D average
answer: Wilke's equation, D<sub>A,m</sub> = (1 − y<sub>A</sub>)/Σ(y<sub>j</sub>/D<sub>Aj</sub>), holds for A diffusing through a mixture whose other species are stagnant; here B, C and D do not move, so it applies.

answer.text: Where the equation comes from: with N<sub>j</sub> = 0 for every j ≠ A, each Stefan–Maxwell term for A reduces to −y<sub>j</sub> N<sub>A</sub>/(c D<sub>Aj</sub>), so
answer.pre:
dy<sub>A</sub>/dz = −(N<sub>A</sub>/c) Σ y<sub>j</sub>/D<sub>Aj</sub> = −N<sub>A</sub> (1 − y<sub>A</sub>)/(c D<sub>A,m</sub>)
which defines D<sub>A,m</sub> = (1 − y<sub>A</sub>)/Σ (y<sub>j</sub>/D<sub>Aj</sub>)

answer: D<sub>A,m</sub> = 0.95/3.42×10⁴ = 2.78×10⁻⁵ m²/s. On an A-free basis (y′_B = 0.421, y′_C = 0.368, y′_D = 0.211) D<sub>A,m</sub> = 1/Σ(y′_j/D<sub>Aj</sub>) gives the same 2.78×10⁻⁵ m²/s.
C has the smallest pair diffusivity and the largest share of the resistance (54 %), so it pulls D<sub>A,m</sub> well below D<sub>AB</sub> even though B is the most abundant partner.

Flux through the stagnant mixture: c = 101325/(8.314 × 300) = 40.6 mol/m³, and N<sub>A</sub> = (c D<sub>A,m</sub>/L) ln[(1 − y<sub>A2</sub>)/(1 − y<sub>A1</sub>)] = (40.6 × 2.78×10⁻⁵/0.0015) × ln(0.99/0.95) = 0.753 × 0.0412 = 3.10×10⁻² mol/(m²·s).
Because B, C and D keep their ratios through the film, D<sub>A,m</sub> stays at 2.78×10⁻⁵ m²/s at every point, and the integration with a constant D is exact here.
A common error is to average D itself: (0.40 × 6.0 + 0.35 × 1.9 + 0.20 × 2.2)×10⁻⁵/0.95 = 3.69×10⁻⁵ m²/s, which would give 4.12×10⁻² mol/(m²·s), 33 % too high.

If the film were not stagnant, for example if B were absorbed alongside A, the terms y<sub>A</sub> N<sub>B</sub>/(c D<sub>AB</sub>) would no longer vanish and Wilke's equation would not apply; the full Stefan–Maxwell set would be needed.
Check: D<sub>A,m</sub> = 2.78×10⁻⁵ lies between the smallest (1.9×10⁻⁵) and largest (6.0×10⁻⁵) pair values, as a weighted resistance sum must.

bank.q: A steel part 10 mm thick, with 0.20 wt% carbon, is carburized from both faces in a gas that holds the surface at 1.20 wt%. At the carburizing temperature D = 1.5×10⁻¹¹ m²/s. Find the time for the carbon to reach 0.80 wt% at 0.50 mm depth, justify the solution used and say how long a 1.0 mm case would take. Take erfc(0.35) = 0.6206 and erfc(0.40) = 0.5716.
answer: This is unsteady diffusion into a solid with a fixed surface value, Fick's second law with constant D. For thin case depths the far side of the part feels nothing, so the semi-infinite solution applies: (c − c₀)/(c<sub>s</sub> − c₀) = erfc[z/(2√(Dt))].

Why erfc: Fick's second law ∂c/∂t = D ∂²c/∂z² with c = c₀ everywhere at t = 0, c = c<sub>s</sub> at the surface for t > 0 and c → c₀ far inside has the similarity variable η = z/(2√(Dt)); its solution is the complementary error function. Carbon is a small interstitial atom in hot austenite, which is why D is as large as 10⁻¹¹ m²/s.

Semi-infinite check: the carbon front reaches about 4√(Dt) = 4 × √(1.5×10⁻¹¹ × 3.03×10⁴) = 4 × 0.67 mm = 2.7 mm, less than the 5 mm half-thickness, so the two fronts do not meet and the solution is valid.

Doubling the depth: t ∝ z² at a fixed concentration ratio, so a 1.0 mm case to the same 0.80 wt% needs 4 × 8.4 = 33.7 h, and its front (about 5.4 mm) would then touch the centre, so the semi-infinite answer becomes only an estimate.

Practical point: since t ∝ z²/D and D follows the Arrhenius law, plants raise the temperature to cut the cycle time; a higher D at a hotter furnace gives the same case depth in a fraction of the hours, at the cost of grain growth in the steel.

Assumptions: D is taken as constant over the carbon range, and each face is treated as a semi-infinite solid. That holds while the penetration depth 2√(Dt) = 2√(1.5×10⁻¹¹ × 30 240) = 1.35 mm stays well below the 5 mm half-thickness; much longer runs would let the two fronts meet, and the centre carbon would then start to rise.
Check: after 10 h, the 0.80 wt% depth is 2 × 0.371 × √(1.5×10⁻¹¹ × 36000) = 0.54 mm, a little beyond 0.50 mm, consistent with 8.4 h.

bank.q: Compare the two-bulb, Winkelmann (Stefan tube) and diaphragm-cell methods for measuring diffusivity, with their assumptions and errors. Then evaluate D from this Winkelmann run for CCl₄ in air at 321 K and 101.3 kPa (vapour pressure 37.6 kPa, ρ<sub>L</sub> = 1540 kg/m³, M = 154 g/mol): level fall z − z₀ = 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 mm after t = 7100, 15780, 26030, 37860, 51270 s.
outline: Slope, D and z₀ from the intercept
Choice of method for a gas and for a liquid
answer: Two-bulb method (gases): two bulbs of volume V joined by a tube of length L and area S start at different compositions; with equimolar counter-diffusion ln(Δy₀/Δy) = (2 D S/(L V)) t, so D comes from the slope. Assumes a pseudo-steady tube and well-mixed bulbs; errors come from temperature drift, leaks and the tube end effects.

Winkelmann method (vapour of a volatile liquid in a gas): the liquid evaporates up a narrow tube into a gas stream that keeps y<sub>A2</sub> = 0 at the top; the fall of the level is read with a travelling microscope. Assumes stagnant gas, a pseudo-steady profile and constant temperature; errors come from convection at the mouth, cooling of the surface by evaporation and reading the level.

Diaphragm cell (liquids): two stirred compartments separated by a porous glass disc; ln(Δc₀/Δc) = β D t. The cell constant β is found by calibration with a known pair (dilute KCl in water). Errors come from poor stirring (films at the disc faces), bubbles in the pores and a wrong calibration.

answer.text: Winkelmann data. With ρ<sub>L</sub>/M · z dz/dt = D c y<sub>A1</sub>/[(y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub>] and the level read from an unknown start z₀:
answer.pre: t/(z − z₀) = [ρ<sub>L</sub> (y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub> / (2 M D c y<sub>A1</sub>)] (z − z₀) + ρ<sub>L</sub> (y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub> z₀/(M D c y<sub>A1</sub>)

answer: The points lie on a straight line; least squares gives slope s = 3.153×10⁷ s/m² and intercept 1.262×10⁶ s/m.

D = ρ<sub>L</sub> (y<sub>B</sub>)<sub>lm</sub>/(2 M c y<sub>A1</sub> s) = 1540 × 0.800/(2 × 0.154 × 37.96 × 0.3712 × 3.153×10⁷) = 9.0×10⁻⁶ m²/s. The intercept over twice the slope gives the starting path z₀ = 1.262×10⁶/(2 × 3.153×10⁷) = 0.020 m, so the level did start 20 mm below the top.

Evaluation: for a vapour in air the Winkelmann method is the simplest (one tube, a thermostat, a microscope) and z₀ need not be known; the two-bulb cell suits two permanent gases; the diaphragm cell is the standard for liquids, where D is 10⁴ times smaller and a Stefan tube would take years. Whatever the method, quote the temperature, because D rises as about T<sup>1.75</sup> in gases.

bank.q: Explain why diffusivities in solids are small and strongly temperature dependent, naming the mechanisms. A gas in a metal has D = 4.41×10⁻¹⁰ m²/s at 673 K and 1.76×10⁻⁹ m²/s at 773 K: find E and D₀, the value at 300 K and what it means for room-temperature use. Contrast diffusion through the pores of a solid.
outline: Lattice hops: interstitial, vacancy; fast paths
Arrhenius law and its log form
E and D₀ from two points
Extrapolation to 300 K and a penetration depth
Porous solids: ε, τ and Knudsen
answer: In a crystalline solid atoms sit on lattice sites; a diffusing atom must jump to a neighbouring site. Small atoms (C, N, H) jump between host atoms (interstitial diffusion); larger ones swap with an empty site (vacancy diffusion). Grain boundaries and surfaces are disordered fast paths with lower barriers. Each jump needs the atom to cross an energy barrier E, and only the fraction exp(−E/RT) of attempts succeed, so D is small and climbs steeply with T.
At 300 K: D = 1.95×10⁻⁵ exp(−59900/(8.314 × 300)) = 7.4×10⁻¹⁶ m²/s, about six orders of magnitude below the 673 K value.

Meaning: the depth reached in one day is about √(Dt) = √(7.4×10⁻¹⁶ × 86400) = 8×10⁻⁶ m, eight micrometres, against about 6 mm at 673 K. Heat treatment and doping are therefore done hot, and a part keeps its case profile at room temperature.

Steady permeation: at 773 K a 5 mm sheet with a concentration difference of 0.45 mol/m³ passes N = 1.76×10⁻⁹ × 0.45/0.005 = 1.6×10⁻⁷ mol/(m²·s). When a gas sets the surface value, c = S p and the flux is D S Δp/L, so the permeability D S, not D alone, decides leakage.

Porous solids are different: the gas moves through the pores, not the solid. The effective diffusivity is D<sub>eff</sub> = ε D/τ, and in pores narrower than the mean free path the Knudsen value D<sub>K</sub> = 97 r (T/M)<sup>1/2</sup> replaces the molecular one. For 5 nm pores at 500 K, D<sub>K</sub> = 2.05×10⁻⁶ m²/s, and with ε = 0.4, τ = 4 the pellet gives about 2×10⁻⁷ m²/s, still far above lattice diffusion. Its temperature dependence is weak (√T), unlike the Arrhenius law.

The two mechanisms differ in size. Interstitial atoms such as hydrogen, carbon and nitrogen jump between gaps in the lattice and need only the energy to squeeze past their neighbours. Substitutional atoms can move only into a vacant site next to them, so their activation energy also includes the energy to form that vacancy, and their diffusivities are smaller by many orders of magnitude at the same temperature.
Check: D₀ exp(−E/(R × 773)) = 1.95×10⁻⁵ × 9.0×10⁻⁵ = 1.76×10⁻⁹ m²/s reproduces the second data point.

bank.q: Evaluate why multicomponent diffusion cannot be handled as independent binary pairs. Present the Stefan–Maxwell equations, show that they reduce to the binary results, derive the condition for Wilke's equation and apply it to A (y<sub>A</sub> = 0.10 falling to 0.02 across a 2.0 mm film) in stagnant B and C (y<sub>B</sub> = 0.30, y<sub>C</sub> = 0.60, B:C fixed at 1:2), with D<sub>AB</sub> = 1.0×10⁻⁵, D<sub>AC</sub> = 3.0×10⁻⁵ m²/s and c = 40.6 mol/m³.
outline: Stefan–Maxwell form and its friction meaning
answer: In an n-component gas every pair has its own diffusivity, n(n − 1)/2 of them (3 for a ternary). The flux of A is braked separately by B and by C, so it depends on the gradients and fluxes of all species. One Fick constant per species cannot capture this; in extreme cases a species can even diffuse against its own gradient.

answer.pre: dy<sub>i</sub>/dz = Σ<sub>j≠i</sub> (y<sub>i</sub> N<sub>j</sub> − y<sub>j</sub> N<sub>i</sub>)/(c D<sub>ij</sub>),   i = 1 … n (n − 1 independent)

answer: Each term is a friction between i and j, proportional to how fast they slip past each other and to 1/D<sub>ij</sub>. For n = 2: c D₁₂ dy₁/dz = y₁N₂ − y₂N₁, which rearranges to N₁ = −c D₁₂ dy₁/dz + y₁(N₁ + N₂), the binary result that contains both the equimolar and stagnant cases.

answer.text: Wilke: put N<sub>j</sub> = 0 for every j ≠ A:
answer.pre:
dy<sub>A</sub>/dz = −N<sub>A</sub> Σ<sub>j≠A</sub> y<sub>j</sub>/(c D<sub>Aj</sub>)
        = −N<sub>A</sub> (1 − y<sub>A</sub>)/(c D<sub>A,m</sub>),   D<sub>A,m</sub> = (1 − y<sub>A</sub>)/Σ y<sub>j</sub>/D<sub>Aj</sub>

answer: So N<sub>A</sub> = −c D<sub>A,m</sub> dy<sub>A</sub>/[(1 − y<sub>A</sub>) dz], the stagnant-film form with D<sub>A,m</sub> in place of D<sub>AB</sub>. If the stagnant species keep their ratios, D<sub>A,m</sub> does not change along the path and the integration is exact.

Numbers: D<sub>A,m</sub> = 0.90/(0.30/1.0×10⁻⁵ + 0.60/3.0×10⁻⁵) = 0.90/5.0×10⁴ = 1.8×10⁻⁵ m²/s. At the other face (y<sub>A</sub> = 0.02, y<sub>B</sub> = 0.3267, y<sub>C</sub> = 0.6533) the same formula gives 1.8×10⁻⁵ m²/s again.

Flux: N<sub>A</sub> = (c D<sub>A,m</sub>/L) ln[(1 − y<sub>A2</sub>)/(1 − y<sub>A1</sub>)] = (40.6 × 1.8×10⁻⁵/0.002) × ln(0.98/0.90) = 0.365 × 0.0852 = 3.11×10⁻² mol/(m²·s). Dropping the bulk term would give 2.92×10⁻² (6 % low); averaging D instead of resistances (2.33×10⁻⁵ m²/s) would give 4.03×10⁻² (30 % high).

Limits: Wilke's equation fails when the other species are not stagnant (for example when B is also absorbed or counter-diffuses), when no species is dilute and the ratios change along the path, and in non-ideal liquids. Then the full Stefan–Maxwell set must be solved, as process simulators do; for a dilute A in a stagnant mixture Wilke is adequate for design.

glossary.def: Change in concentration per unit distance; it drives diffusion.
Moles of a species divided by total moles in the mixture.
Mass of a species divided by total mass of the mixture.
A mixture containing only two species.
Motion of the mixture as a whole, carrying all species with it.
Mass transfer between a flowing fluid and a surface or another phase.
Moles of a species crossing unit area per unit time relative to the mixture velocity.
Moles of a species crossing a fixed plane per unit area per unit time.
The proportionality constant between diffusion flux and concentration gradient.
Condition in which concentration at a fixed point does not change with time.
Condition in which concentration at a fixed point changes with time.
A medium thick enough that the far boundary has no effect during the observed time.
A stated concentration or flux at the surface of the diffusion path.
The concentration field at time zero.
An apparent D for a porous solid that includes porosity and tortuosity effects.
Diffusion through gas-filled or liquid-filled pores in a solid.
Pore diffusion in which molecule-wall collisions dominate over molecule-molecule collisions.
Movement of adsorbed molecules along the wall of a pore.
Faster diffusion along boundaries between grains in a solid.
Small atoms hop between lattice sites without displacing host atoms.
An atom moves into an empty lattice site, so the vacancy moves the other way.
Adding carbon to the surface of steel by diffusion at high temperature.
Adding a controlled impurity to silicon by diffusion to change its electrical behaviour.
A factor greater than one that accounts for the longer crooked path through pores.
The energy barrier that makes solid diffusion rise steeply with temperature.
Measuring the diffusivity of a vapour from the slow fall of the liquid level in a narrow tube swept at the top by a gas.
Molar volume of a liquid at its normal boiling point, estimated by adding atomic increments; used in Wilke–Chang.
